title: Perceived age-friendliness in multiethnic and multigenerational Klang Valley, Malaysia: An extended WHO Age-Friendly Cities assessment
content:
by Sin Meun How, Mohammad Mujaheed Hassan, Zalina Shari

Malaysia’s transition towards an ageing society underscores the need for context-sensitive tools to assess urban age-friendliness, particularly in the multiethnic cities of the Global South. This quantitative cross-sectional study adapted and extended the World Health Organization’s Age-Friendly Cities framework by incorporating additional domains on technology and financial situation to assess perceived neighbourhood age-friendliness across six local authorities in Klang Valley, Malaysia. Incorporating a multigenerational perspective, the study captured perceptions from diverse age and ethnic populations. A bilingual self-administered questionnaire consisting of 15 socio-demographic items and 75 closed-ended age-friendly indicators measured on a 5-point Likert scale was administered to 511 community-dwelling adults aged 18 years and above. The instrument underwent expert review, content validity assessment, and pilot testing prior to implementation. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, one-sample t-tests, independent samples t-tests, and one-way ANOVA. The overall age-friendly score (AFI) indicated that Klang Valley was generally age-friendly, with scores significantly above the neutral midpoint of the 5-point scale (M = 3.36, p < .001). The technology and respect and social inclusion domains recorded the highest mean scores (both M = 3.77, p < .001), while civic participation and employment was the only domain scoring significantly below the midpoint (M = 2.81, p < .001). Significant spatial differences were observed across local authorities for AFI and nine domains (p < .05), with Putrajaya, the master-planned administrative capital consistently reporting the highest scores. Ethnic differences were significant for AFI and eight domains (p < .05). In contrast, age-group differences were largely non-significant except for technology, where young adult respondents reported higher satisfaction than older adult respondents (p < .001). The findings suggest that perceived age-friendliness in Klang Valley varies more clearly by spatial and ethnic contexts than by chronological age. This study provides a multidomain empirical benchmark of urban age-friendliness in Malaysia from a person-environment fit perspective. It highlights the importance of inclusive, multigenerational, and digitally responsive urban planning strategies.
